newsitem.title: GERMANY: German official rates now bottomed - Reuter survey.
newsitem.headline: German official rates now bottomed - Reuter survey.

text.p: German long-term and official interest rates have now bottomed and will start to head higher this year, with the Bundesbank likely to raise the official rates at the turn of the year, a Reuter poll showed.

But according to the survey of 33 economists, the upturn in credit costs will be only gradual, with most of those who gave forecasts seeing the discount rate rising to no more than three percent by the end of 1998 from 2.50 percent currently.
Only one institution, the Frankfurter Sparkasse, predicted a further cut in the discount rate in this rate cycle. It said the rate would fall to two percent in the second quarter 1997.

The survey, which was conducted in the middle of last week, did not call for specific forecasts on the securities repurchase rate, the Bundesbank's main money market rate which some economists believe could still be cut this cycle.
Economic data released in the last week, since the survey was conducted, has given weight to the view that there could be another cut in the repo rate, which now stands at three percent.

The three-month Frankfurt interbank offered rate (FIBOR) was seen holding steady close to the current level of about 3.10 percent for first six months of 1997, according to the mean forecast, and then rising steadily to reach 3.91 percent at the end of 1998.

Long-term rates -- based on the 10-year benchmark government bond yield -- were seen rising from an average forecast level of 5.94 percent in the first quarter of this year to 6.57 percent in the final quarter of 1998.

The overall survey showed little need for major changes in Bundesbank policy over the next two years, with inflation seen remaining weak and M3 money supply growth seen remaining close to the Bundesbank's target.
M3, the Bundesbank's main monetary policy indicator, was seen holding on a steady course over the next year, remaining within the Bundesbank's 3-1/2 to 6-1/2 percent 1997 growth corridor.
The mean forecast showed annualised M3 growth holding steady at 5.6 percent at the end of each quarter next year.
